a: God finds fault with them when he says
t: Fault with them, or with it?
p: One letter decides whether God faults the people or the covenant.

readings.w: SBL, NA28, NA27, Westcott-Hort
readings.en: finding fault with them, he says
readings.plain: God finds fault with them when he says

readings.w: Tyndale House (THGNT), Tregelles, Byzantine text (Robinson-Pierpont), Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.en: finding fault, he says to them
readings.plain: God finds fault with it when he says to them

why: The accusative 'them' is printed by most critical editions and makes the people the object of blame, which matches Jeremiah's own words, 'They broke that covenant of mine' (Jeremiah 31:32). The dative can be read the same way ('finding fault with them'), so the difference may be one of spelling more than meaning.
b: The verb memphomai can take either case. Read with the dative as 'to them', the sentence blames the first covenant (8:7) and God speaks to the people. The writer holds both thoughts: the first covenant could not make perfect (7:19), and the people did not stay in it (8:9).

p: Nearly all manuscripts say 'fellow citizen'; a few, and the KJV's Greek, say 'neighbor'.

readings.w: P46 (about AD 200), Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, Claromontanus and most manuscripts; the Byzantine text; SBL, NA28, Tyndale House
A few manuscripts (among them P, 81, 104); Textus Receptus (KJV 'neighbour')

why: 'Fellow citizen' has by far the strongest and oldest support and is the reading of Swete's Septuagint of Jeremiah. 'Neighbor' looks like a scribe's change to the more familiar word, the one in the Hebrew of Jeremiah 31:34 and in the command to love one's neighbor.

p: The Byzantine text adds 'and their lawless deeds', from the form of the quotation in 10:17.

readings.w: SBL, NA28, Tyndale House (THGNT), Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
Byzantine text (Robinson-Pierpont), Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.orig: καὶ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν αὐτῶν καὶ τῶν ἀνομιῶν αὐτῶν
readings.en: and their sins and their lawless deeds
readings.plain: their sins and their lawless deeds

why: The shorter reading matches Jeremiah's Greek (38:34) and is printed by all the critical editions. The longer one adds the words the writer himself uses when he repeats the quotation in 10:17, a natural change for a copyist. The KJV has 'their sins and their iniquities'.

a: Now the first covenant also had
t: The first covenant, or the first tent?
p: The SBL leaves out 'also'; the Textus Receptus adds 'tent', though the KJV supplies 'covenant'.

readings.w: NA28, NA27, Tyndale House (THGNT), Westcott-Hort, Tregelles, Byzantine text (Robinson-Pierpont)
readings.orig: εἶχε μὲν οὖν καὶ ἡ πρώτη
readings.plain: Now the first covenant also had

readings.w: SBL (following the margin of Westcott-Hort)
Textus Receptus
readings.orig: εἶχε μὲν οὖν καὶ ἡ πρώτη σκηνή
readings.en: now the first tent also had
readings.plain: Now the first tent also had

why: Here the Plain English Translation departs from its base text, the SBL, and keeps 'also', which every other edition prints. The Greek says only 'the first'; 8:13 has just spoken of the first covenant, so 'covenant' is understood. The Textus Receptus adds 'tent' (skēnē), but the KJV, translated from it, supplies 'covenant' in italics ('the first [covenant] had also').

a: the good things that have now come
t: Good things that have come, or are to come?
p: The oldest papyrus and Vaticanus say the good things 'have come'; Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus say 'are to come'.

readings.w: P46 (about AD 200), Vaticanus (first hand), Claromontanus (first hand), minuscules 1611, 1739 and 2005, Old Latin d and e, Syriac (the Peshitta and the Harclean text); SBL, NA28, Westcott-Hort
readings.en: of the good things that have come
readings.plain: the good things that have now come

readings.w: Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, a corrector of Claromontanus, the Latin versions (apart from Old Latin d and e), the Harclean Syriac margin, the Coptic versions; Tyndale House (THGNT), Tregelles, Byzantine text (Robinson-Pierpont), Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.en: of the good things to come

why: Both readings are early and both are well supported. 'That have come' has the oldest witness (P46) and Vaticanus, and is the harder reading, since 10:1 speaks of 'the good things to come' and a scribe could easily have copied that phrase here. 'To come' fits 10:1 and is printed by the Tyndale House edition. The difference is small in Greek (genomenōn / mellontōn) and large in meaning: are the good things already here in Christ, or still ahead?
b: Sebastian Fuhrmann, who argues for 'that have come', lists the witnesses in his 2008 article in Biblica, in one footnote, which is the only source of the manuscript lists here; the edition lists come from the SBL apparatus and the word list. Hebrews holds both sides: believers 'have tasted ... the powers of the age to come' (6:5) and still wait for 'the city that is coming' (13:14).

p: The editions divide between 'our' and 'your'; the KJV has 'your'.

readings.w: SBL, NA28, NA27, Westcott-Hort
Tyndale House (THGNT), Tregelles, Byzantine text (Robinson-Pierpont), Textus Receptus (KJV)

why: In Greek of this period the two words (hēmōn, hymōn) sounded alike and were easily confused. The Plain English Translation follows SBL and NA28. The meaning hardly changes: the writer includes himself with his hearers ('we') through most of the sermon.

p: The SBL edition alone leaves out 'and the goats'; the other editions keep it.

readings.w: NA28, NA27, Tyndale House (THGNT), Westcott-Hort, Tregelles; Byzantine text (Robinson-Pierpont) and Textus Receptus (KJV) without the second 'the' (kai tragōn)
readings.en: of the calves and the goats

readings.w: SBL

why: Here the Plain English Translation departs from its base text, the SBL, and follows NA28 and the Tyndale House edition. The words are in every other edition. A scribe may have added them from 9:12 ('goats and calves'), or dropped them because Exodus 24:5 mentions only bulls. Either way the scene is the same.

a: the law can never make perfect
t: The law can never, or they can never?
p: Singular or plural verb: the law cannot make perfect, or the sacrifices cannot.

readings.w: SBL, NA28, NA27, Textus Receptus
readings.plain: the law can never make perfect

readings.w: Tyndale House (THGNT), Westcott-Hort, Tregelles, Byzantine text
readings.en: they (the priests or the sacrifices) are able

why: The singular makes 'the law' the subject of the whole sentence, which is how it begins. The plural, printed by Tyndale House, makes the priests who offer, or the sacrifices, the subject, and is the smoother Greek. Either way the point is the same: the yearly offerings could not bring the worshipers to the goal.

a: I have come to do your will
p: The Byzantine text and the KJV repeat 'O God' from 10:7.

readings.w: SBL, NA28, Tyndale House (THGNT), Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
readings.orig: ἰδοὺ ἥκω τοῦ ποιῆσαι τὸ θέλημά σου
readings.en: look, I have come to do your will
readings.plain: I have come to do your will

readings.w: Byzantine text (Robinson-Pierpont), Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.orig: ἰδοὺ ἥκω τοῦ ποιῆσαι, ὁ θεός, τὸ θέλημά σου
readings.en: look, I have come to do your will, O God
readings.plain: I have come to do your will, O God

why: The writer repeats the quotation in a shortened form to make his point; a copyist filled in 'O God' from 10:7. The critical editions leave it out.

p: A few early witnesses read 'every high priest'; most read 'every priest'.

readings.w: P46, Sinaiticus, Claromontanus, the Byzantine text and most manuscripts; SBL, NA28, Tyndale House
Alexandrinus, Ephraemi, and a number of later manuscripts; Syriac, Coptic, Armenian and Ethiopic versions

why: 'Priest' has the oldest papyrus and the widest support, and it fits the point: the daily offerings were made by ordinary priests. 'High priest' is the word Hebrews has used through chapters 8-9, so a scribe could easily have written it here.

p: The Byzantine text and the KJV add 'says the Lord' after 'I will pay back', as in Romans 12:19.

readings.w: SBL, NA28, Tyndale House (THGNT), Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
readings.en: I will pay back. And again

readings.w: Byzantine text (Robinson-Pierpont), Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.orig: ἐγὼ ἀνταποδώσω, λέγει κύριος· καὶ πάλιν
readings.en: I will pay back, says the Lord. And again

why: Paul's quotation of the same words ends 'says the Lord' (Romans 12:19), and a copyist likely brought the phrase in from there. The critical editions leave it out.

t: The prisoners, or 'me in my chains'?
p: The critical text reads 'the prisoners'; the Byzantine text and the KJV read 'my chains', which seemed to show Paul as author.

readings.w: SBL, NA28, NA27, Tyndale House (THGNT), Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
Byzantine text (Robinson-Pierpont), Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.plain: You felt for me in my chains

why: All the critical editions read 'the prisoners'. The two Greek words differ by a few letters (desmiois / desmois mou). The reading 'my chains' would make the writer a prisoner known to the readers, which fit the old belief that Paul wrote Hebrews (compare Philippians 1:7). 13:3 asks the readers to keep caring for 'the prisoners', with the same word.

a: a better possession of your own
p: Two editions leave out 'better'; the Byzantine text and the KJV add 'in heaven'.

readings.w: SBL, NA28, NA27, Tregelles
readings.en: that you yourselves have a better possession
readings.plain: a better possession of your own

readings.w: Tyndale House (THGNT), Westcott-Hort
readings.en: that you yourselves have a possession

readings.w: Byzantine text (Robinson-Pierpont), Textus Receptus (KJV); the Textus Receptus also has 'in' before 'yourselves' (KJV 'knowing in yourselves')
readings.orig: ἔχειν ἑαυτοῖς κρείττονα ὕπαρξιν ἐν οὐρανοῖς
readings.en: that you have for yourselves a better possession in heaven
readings.plain: a better possession of your own in heaven

why: 'Better' (kreittona) is printed by the SBL, the Nestle-Aland editions, Tregelles and the Byzantine text; the Tyndale House edition and Westcott-Hort leave it out. It is the book's key word (1:4; 7:22; 8:6; 11:16, 35, 40), which could explain a scribe adding it, or its loss could be a slip. 'In heaven' explains where the possession is; it is missing from the critical editions. The meaning matches 11:16 and 13:14.

p: The critical editions read 'my righteous one'; the Byzantine text and the KJV read 'the righteous' (or 'the just').

readings.w: SBL, NA28, NA27, Tyndale House (THGNT), Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
Byzantine text (Robinson-Pierpont), Textus Receptus (KJV)

why: The editions agree on 'my'. Copyists may have dropped it to make Hebrews match Paul's quotation of the same verse (Romans 1:17; Galatians 3:11). Swete's Septuagint has 'my' in yet another place, 'by my faith', so three forms of Habakkuk 2:4 were in circulation.

t: He still speaks, or he is still spoken of?
p: The Byzantine text and the Textus Receptus read 'he is still spoken of'.

readings.w: SBL, NA28, NA27, Tyndale House (THGNT), Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
Byzantine text (Robinson-Pierpont), Textus Receptus

why: The active 'speaks' matches 12:24, where Jesus' blood 'speaks better than Abel', and Genesis 4:10, where Abel's blood cries out. The passive changes the meaning: Abel is talked about. The KJV, though made from the Textus Receptus, has 'yet speaketh'.

a: together with Sarah herself, he received power to father children, even past the age for it, since he regarded the one who had promised as trustworthy.
t: Abraham with Sarah, or Sarah herself?
p: All editions have the same letters; the SBL editor reads them as 'with Sarah herself' (Abraham as subject), the others as 'Sarah herself'.

readings.w: SBL (Michael Holmes's choice of accents, following the margin of Westcott-Hort; the SBL apparatus names no manuscript for it)
readings.orig: πίστει καὶ αὐτῇ Σάρρᾳ δύναμιν εἰς καταβολὴν σπέρματος ἔλαβεν καὶ παρὰ καιρὸν ἡλικίας
readings.en: by faith, with Sarah herself, he received power to lay down seed, even beyond the time of life
readings.plain: together with Sarah herself, he received power to father children, even past the age for it, since he regarded the one who had promised as trustworthy.

readings.w: Westcott-Hort (text), Tregelles
readings.orig: πίστει καὶ αὐτὴ Σάρρα δύναμιν εἰς καταβολὴν σπέρματος ἔλαβεν
readings.en: by faith Sarah herself received power to conceive
readings.plain: Sarah herself received power to conceive, even past the age for it, since she regarded the one who had promised as trustworthy.

readings.w: NA28 and NA27, which add 'barren' (στεῖρα)
readings.orig: πίστει καὶ αὐτὴ Σάρρα στεῖρα δύναμιν εἰς καταβολὴν σπέρματος ἔλαβεν
readings.en: by faith Sarah herself, barren, received power to conceive
readings.plain: Sarah herself, though barren, received power to conceive, even past the age for it, since she regarded the one who had promised as trustworthy.

readings.w: Byzantine text (Robinson-Pierpont), Textus Receptus (KJV), which add 'gave birth'
readings.orig: πίστει καὶ αὐτὴ Σάρρα δύναμιν ... ἔλαβεν, καὶ παρὰ καιρὸν ἡλικίας ἔτεκεν
readings.en: by faith Sarah herself received power to conceive, and gave birth past the time of life
readings.plain: Sarah herself received power to conceive, and she gave birth even past the age for it, since she regarded the one who had promised as trustworthy.

why: Early manuscripts were written without accents or iota subscripts, so 'Sarah herself' (subject) and 'with Sarah herself' (dative) are the same letters; the choice is the editor's, not a manuscript's. The SBL editor, following Westcott and Hort's margin, prints the dative, and the Plain English Translation follows its base text here because the phrase 'power for the laying down of seed' (dynamin eis katabolēn spermatos) is used of a father's part, not a mother's, and 11:12 goes on 'from one man'. Every other edition makes Sarah the subject, and so do most Bibles, the KJV among them ('Sara herself received strength to conceive seed'). NA28 also prints 'barren', which the Plain English Translation's reading does not have.
b: Readers on both sides agree that Genesis gives both Abraham and Sarah moments of doubt (Genesis 17:17; 18:12) and of trust (Genesis 15:6; 21:6). The added 'barren' in NA28 and 'gave birth' in the Byzantine text each make the verse read smoothly with Sarah as subject. See the topic on Sarah.

p: The Textus Receptus alone adds 'and were persuaded of them', which the KJV prints.

readings.w: SBL, NA28, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles, Byzantine text
Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.en: seeing and being persuaded of them and greeting them
readings.plain: and were persuaded of it, and greeted it

why: The words are missing from the Byzantine text as well as the critical editions; they are found in the printed Textus Receptus that stands behind the KJV ('and were persuaded of them, and embraced them').

a: They died by murder with the sword
p: Some editions add 'they were tested' after 'they were sawed in two'.

readings.w: SBL, NA28, NA27, Tregelles
readings.en: they were sawed in two, they died by murder of the sword
readings.plain: They died by murder with the sword

readings.w: Tyndale House (THGNT), Westcott-Hort, Byzantine text (Robinson-Pierpont), Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.orig: ἐπρίσθησαν, ἐπειράσθησαν, ἐν φόνῳ μαχαίρης ἀπέθανον
readings.en: they were sawed in two, they were tested, they died by the sword
readings.plain: They were tested. They died by murder with the sword

why: 'They were tested' (epeirasthēsan) is a weak climax in a list of violent deaths, and it looks very like 'they were sawn' (epristhēsan) or 'they were burned' (eprēsthēsan), so it may be an accidental double or a change of an earlier word. Yet the Tyndale House edition and Westcott-Hort print it, and the KJV has 'were tempted'. The Plain English Translation follows SBL and NA28 in leaving it out.

p: The editions divide: 'against himself' (NA28, Tyndale House) or 'against themselves' (SBL, Westcott-Hort).

readings.w: NA28, NA27, Tyndale House (THGNT), Tregelles; the Byzantine text and Textus Receptus have εἰς αὐτόν, the same meaning
SBL, Westcott-Hort

why: Here the Plain English Translation departs from its base text, the SBL, and follows NA28 and Tyndale House. 'Against themselves' is the harder reading and has been defended for that reason: those who opposed Jesus were really harming themselves (compare the rebels of Numbers 16, "these men who sinned at the cost of their lives" (Numbers 16:38)). But 'against himself' fits the call to 'think of the one who put up with so much', and the KJV reads it too.

a: What you are enduring is for your discipline. God is dealing with you as his sons.
t: For discipline, or if you endure discipline?
p: The Textus Receptus and the KJV read 'If ye endure chastening'.

readings.w: SBL, Nestle 1904, Westcott-Hort, Tischendorf, Byzantine text (Robinson-Pierpont)
readings.plain: What you are enduring is for your discipline. God is dealing with you as his sons.

readings.w: Textus Receptus (Stephanus 1550, Scrivener 1894; KJV), the 1904 Greek Orthodox Church text
readings.plain: If you endure discipline, God is dealing with you as his sons.

why: The two readings differ by one letter (eis / ei). The critical editions and the Byzantine text read 'for discipline': the readers' sufferings are themselves God's training. The Textus Receptus makes it a condition.

t: A mountain that can be touched
p: The Byzantine text and the KJV add 'mountain'.

readings.w: SBL, NA28, Tyndale House (THGNT), Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
Byzantine text (Robinson-Pierpont), Textus Receptus (KJV)

why: The critical editions leave the mountain unnamed, which matches 12:22, where 'Mount Zion' is named. Copyists added 'mountain' to make the contrast explicit; the meaning is the same. The Byzantine text also reads 'darkness' (skotos) where the critical text has 'gloom' (zophos).

p: The Textus Receptus adds 'or shot through with an arrow' from Exodus 19:13; the KJV prints it.

readings.w: SBL, NA28, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles, Byzantine text
Textus Receptus (KJV 'or thrust through with a dart')
readings.en: it will be stoned or shot down with an arrow
readings.plain: must be stoned or shot through with an arrow

why: The extra words complete the quotation found in Swete's Septuagint of Exodus 19:13 (ē bolidi katatoxeuthēsetai). They are missing from the Byzantine text as well as from the critical editions.

p: The Textus Receptus and the KJV read 'speaketh better things'.

readings.w: SBL, NA28, NA27, Tyndale House (THGNT), Westcott-Hort, Tregelles, Byzantine text (Robinson-Pierpont)
Textus Receptus (KJV)

why: The singular 'better' (used as an adverb) is printed by every edition but the Textus Receptus. The plural makes the comparison about the things said rather than the way the blood speaks; the meaning is close.

t: I will shake, or I shake?
p: The Byzantine text, the Textus Receptus and the KJV read 'I shake' (present).

readings.w: SBL, NA28, NA27, Tyndale House (THGNT), Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
Byzantine text (Robinson-Pierpont), Textus Receptus (KJV)

why: The future matches the Septuagint of Haggai 2:6 (Swete's edition: seisō) and the promise Hebrews draws from it. The present may be a copying slip or a way of making the shaking already under way.

t: Let us worship, or we worship?
p: The Byzantine text and the Tyndale House edition read 'by which we worship' (indicative).

readings.w: SBL, NA28, NA27, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles, Textus Receptus (KJV 'whereby we may serve')
Byzantine text (Robinson-Pierpont), Tyndale House (THGNT)

why: The two forms differ by one vowel (ō / o), which sounded alike. The subjunctive continues 'let us give thanks'; the indicative states what thankfulness does.

t: Reverence and dread, or modesty and reverence?
p: The Byzantine text and the KJV read 'with reverence and godly fear' (aidous kai eulabeias).

readings.w: SBL, NA28, NA27, Tyndale House (THGNT), Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
Byzantine text (Robinson-Pierpont), Textus Receptus (KJV 'with reverence and godly fear')

why: 'Dread' (deos) is found nowhere else in the New Testament, and its strength fits 12:29, 'a devouring fire'. The softer pair 'modesty and reverence' may have been an easier wording. The Plain English Translation's 'reverence' renders eulabeia in both readings, as in 5:7.

t: Every good thing, or every good work?
p: Some editions and the KJV read 'every good work'.

readings.w: SBL, NA28, NA27, Tyndale House (THGNT), Westcott-Hort
Tregelles, Byzantine text (Robinson-Pierpont), Textus Receptus (KJV)

why: The shorter reading is printed by most critical editions; 'work' may come from similar phrases in Paul (2 Corinthians 9:8; 2 Thessalonians 2:17). One manuscript, Alexandrinus, has a longer form, 'every work and word'.

p: The critical editions read 'in us'; Tregelles, the Byzantine text and the KJV read 'in you'.

readings.w: SBL, NA28, NA27, Tyndale House (THGNT), Westcott-Hort
Tregelles, Byzantine text (Robinson-Pierpont), Textus Receptus (KJV)

why: As in 9:14, the two pronouns sounded alike. 'You' matches 'fit you out' earlier in the sentence, which is why copyists might have written it; 'us' is the reading of the critical editions.

p: Nearly all editions read 'to the ages of the ages'; the SBL edition reads only 'to the ages'.

readings.w: NA28, NA27, Tyndale House (THGNT), Westcott-Hort, Tregelles, Byzantine text (Robinson-Pierpont), Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.en: to the ages of the ages

readings.w: SBL

why: Here the Plain English Translation departs from its base text and follows the other editions. A copyist could have lengthened the doxology to the familiar form, which favors the SBL's shorter text; but all the other editions print the longer form.

a: Grace be with all of you.
t: The ending: Amen, and a note added later
p: Some editions add 'Amen'; the Textus Receptus adds a closing note: 'written to the Hebrews from Italy through Timothy'.

readings.w: SBL, NA28, NA27, Westcott-Hort
readings.plain: Grace be with all of you.

readings.w: Tyndale House (THGNT), Tregelles, Byzantine text
readings.orig: ἡ χάρις μετὰ πάντων ὑμῶν. ἀμήν.
readings.en: Grace with all of you. Amen.
readings.plain: Grace be with all of you. Amen.

readings.w: Textus Receptus, which adds a closing note after the letter
readings.orig: ἡ χάρις μετὰ πάντων ὑμῶν. ἀμήν. πρὸς Ἑβραίους ἐγράφη ἀπὸ τῆς Ἰταλίας διὰ Τιμοθέου.
readings.en: Grace with all of you. Amen. To the Hebrews, written from Italy through Timothy.
readings.plain: Grace be with all of you. Amen. [To the Hebrews, written from Italy, through Timothy.]

why: 'Amen' at the end of a letter was often added by copyists, since it was said aloud when the letter was read in church; the editions divide. The closing note in the Textus Receptus is not part of the letter but a later scribe's heading and guess, based on 13:23-24. It reads 'from Italy', which takes the 'those from Italy' of 13:24 as people in Italy.
